{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Sarcoidosis", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic urticaria with associated peripheral neuropathy (e.g., autoimmune urticarial neuropathy syndrome)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Lepromatous leprosy", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)", "confidence": 0.63}, {"diagnosis": "Vitamin B12 deficiency", "confidence": 0.59}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The chronic (>12 months), pruritic rash involving upper body and face—plus new-onset bilateral palmar paresthesias—suggests a systemic process with cutaneous and peripheral nerve involvement. Sarcoidosis is highly plausible: it commonly presents with chronic papular or maculopapular facial/upper trunk rash (e.g., lupus pernio or erythema nodosum variants) and can cause small-fiber or mononeuritis multiplex neuropathy, including palmar paresthesias; serum ACE, chest imaging, and skin biopsy would be key next steps. Chronic urticaria with neuropathy is increasingly recognized as an autoimmune paraneoplastic or idiopathic syndrome—urticarial lesions may become persistent and lichenified over time, and anti-nerve antibodies (e.g., anti-MAG, anti-ganglioside) may coexist. Lepromatous leprosy must be considered in endemic areas or with travel history: it causes symmetric, hypopigmented/erythematous, anesthetic or hypoesthetic plaques on face/trunk and early, symmetric sensory neuropathy (including palmar involvement); slit-skin smear and PCR are confirmatory. Mycosis fungoides (early patch/plaque stage) can mimic chronic eczema or psoriasis, often with facial sparing—but poikiloderma, folliculocentricity, and progressive induration raise suspicion; T-cell receptor clonality on skin biopsy is diagnostic. Vitamin B12 deficiency is less likely given the prominent pruritic rash (not typical) but remains possible: it causes subacute combined degeneration and distal paresthesias, and rare reports link it to chronic urticaria or atrophic dermatitis; however, rash is usually not primary or prominent. Other considerations (e.g., Sjögren’s, celiac, paraneoplastic syndromes) were ranked lower due to lack of supporting features (e.g., sicca, diarrhea, weight loss)."}

Lepromatous leprosy is top-ranked due to its classic triad of chronic hypopigmented/erythematous skin lesions, symmetric sensory neuropathy (often starting in hands/feet), and histopathologic hallmark of acid-fast bacilli within foamy macrophages—though the biopsy result is unspecified, the clinical pattern is highly characteristic and epidemiologically plausible even in non-endemic areas given diagnostic delays. Cutaneous sarcoidosis with neurosarcoidosis ranks second: sarcoid can present with chronic papular/plaque rash (e.g., lupus pernio or maculopapular lesions) and subclinical or overt peripheral neuropathy (including small-fiber or multifocal neuropathies); ACE elevation or hilar adenopathy would support this but are not reported. Chronic cutaneous lupus (e.g., discoid or tumid) may cause scaly, photosensitive facial rash and occasionally co-occur with peripheral neuropathy (especially in overlap syndromes), though paresthesias are less prominent than in leprosy or sarcoid. Sjögren syndrome is included for its association with xeroderma, palpable purpura/vasculitic rash, and high prevalence of sensory-predominant neuropathy (e.g., small-fiber or carpal tunnel), though classic sicca symptoms are unmentioned. GPA is lower-confidence: while it can cause palpable purpura and mononeuritis multiplex, the symmetric palmar paresthesias and year-long indolent course are atypical; granulomatous skin lesions are less common than in sarcoid or leprosy. Other considerations (e.g., psoriasis, contact dermatitis, idiopathic small-fiber neuropathy) were excluded due to lack of symmetry, chronicity, and concurrent cutaneous + neurological features."}

Lepromatous leprosy is top-ranked due to its classic presentation: chronic widespread macular/papular itchy rash, facial involvement (e.g., 'leonine facies'), and early symmetric peripheral neuropathy (often starting in hands/feet); acid-fast bacilli in foamy macrophages would be diagnostic, but absence of stain results does not exclude it—sensitivity of ZN stain in paucibacillary or early lepromatous cases can be low, and PCR or slit-skin smear may be needed. Cutaneous sarcoidosis with neurosarcoidosis is highly plausible given the chronic granulomatous dermatosis and neurologic symptoms (neurosarcoid commonly affects cranial nerves and peripheral nerves, including carpal tunnel-like presentations). Sjögren syndrome fits the chronic inflammatory skin rash (e.g., annular erythema, vasculitic lesions) and sensory neuropathy, though palmar-predominant paresthesia is atypical. Secondary syphilis can cause widespread rash and early neurological involvement (e.g., tabes dorsalis or peripheral neuropathy), but palmar paresthesia alone is less characteristic than more proximal or asymmetric findings; serology would clarify. Chronic urticaria is included as a common mimic for chronic pruritic rash, but it does not explain neuropathy—hence low confidence unless coincident (e.g., idiopathic carpal tunnel), making it the least likely primary unifying diagnosis."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Lepromatous leprosy", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Borderline lepromatous leprosy", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Tuberculoid leprosy", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Sarcoidosis", "confidence": 0.42}, {"diagnosis": "Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)", "confidence": 0.38}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.52, "reasoning": "Chronic itchy rash on upper body and face plus symmetric palmar paresthesias strongly suggest a neurocutaneous process with peripheral nerve involvement. Leprosy is the prototypical disease fulfilling both criteria: skin lesions (often hypopigmented, anesthetic, or pruritic) and distal sensory neuropathy (e.g., palmar numbness/tingling), frequently with dermal nerve infiltration by macrophages. The absence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining results in the log does not rule out leprosy—especially in borderline or tuberculoid forms where AFB are scarce—but lepromatous and borderline lepromatous forms typically show abundant AFB in foamy macrophages; their absence lowers but does not eliminate confidence due to sampling or technical limitations. Granulomatous inflammation with nerve infiltration is highly characteristic of leprosy across spectra. Sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous granulomas and rarely peripheral neuropathy, but palmar paresthesias are atypical and neurologic involvement is uncommon without systemic disease. Mycosis fungoides may present with chronic pruritic patches/plaques and rarely peripheral neuropathy (paraneoplastic or treatment-related), but nerve infiltration is not histopathologic hallmark and palmar involvement is unusual. Confidence scores reflect clinical-epidemiologic likelihood (leprosy highest in endemic areas or with exposure history), histopathologic specificity (nerve-infiltrating granulomas strongly favor leprosy), and symptom concordance (chronicity, distribution, and dual cutaneous + small-fiber neuropathic features)."}
